text: A nitpick - why does this card says "seven steps" when we list nine? Let's rephrase this title so we don't need to correct it every time the detail is refined and the step numbers change. The point of this decision is indeed a pipeline split into well-defined sequential and grouped step graph (vs. its alternative).
New session 4ff154ae.
node src/cli.ts show st-six; node src/cli.ts retitle --help 2>&1 | head -20

card st-six  [decided]
Seven steps, grouped into plan, build, validate
why: Seven named steps sit inside the three stages from #stages.
subtree: 31 cards, 1 open, 30 decided

```
PLAN              BUILD              VALIDATE
intent            implement          measure
options           validate           analyse
prototype         fix
plan
```

Build's middle step and the VALIDATE stage share the word validate. One is a step inside build — the change compiles, its own tests pass, before anything ships. The other is the stage after build — measure and analyse, against production. Worth a distinct name for the step once it's detailed, so the word does not carry two meanings on one diagram.

Each stage's steps get their own subcard — see #st-build-steps and #st-validate-steps.

  -> refines         stages  Three stages: plan, build, validate
  -> supported_by    st-six:ex0  
  <- depends_on      st-tier  A risk tier decides which gates wait for a human
  <- refines         st-build-steps  Build: a builder loop per ticket and a merge loop per run  (29 cards, 29 decided)
  <- refines         st-validate-steps  Validate's two steps, in detail
  <- alternative_to  st-six:opt0  Three stages with no named steps: one model per stage organises its own work

I added the option `stages:opt0` and linked it `alternative_to` #stages. It is a proposal, so it waits for your ✓ on the card.

The option's `why_not` says the rejection depends on model capability. The staged design holds only until a more capable model makes an unstaged run reliable. This is the fact you want to revisit with a newer model.
